related_questions.question: What is the leading cause of COPD?

text_blocks.snippet: The leading cause of COPD (Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease) is tobacco smoke, primarily from cigarette smoking. Other contributing factors include exposure to air pollutants, both in the environment and the workplace, and a family history of COPD.

list.title: Smoking:
list.snippet: Smoking cigarettes is the primary risk factor for COPD, accounting for the vast majority of cases.

list.title: Environmental and Occupational Exposure:
list.snippet: Long-term exposure to air pollutants like dust, fumes, and chemicals can also contribute to COPD. This can occur in workplaces (e.g., coal dust, silica dust) or from household products.

list.title: Secondhand Smoke:
list.snippet: Exposure to secondhand smoke can also increase the risk of developing COPD.

list.title: Family History:
list.snippet: A family history of COPD can also increase an individual's susceptibility to the disease.

list.title: Asthma:
list.snippet: Individuals with asthma may also have an increased risk of developing COPD.

related_questions.question: Is emphysema an upper or lower airway obstruction?
related_questions.snippet: Most commonly emphysema refers to the permanent enlargement of air spaces (alveoli) in the lungs, and is also known as pulmonary emphysema. Emphysema is a lower respiratory tract disease, characterised by enlarged air-filled spaces in the lungs, that can vary in size and may be very large.

related_questions.question: What's the difference between COPD and bronchitis?
related_questions.snippet: Acute bronchitis is typically caused by a virus or, less frequently, bacteria. It's an infection that will clear up after a few weeks. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), on the other hand, is chronic, which means it develops over time. While symptoms may improve, they'll never disappear completely.

related_questions.question: Why does COPD reduce the efficiency of gas exchange in the lungs?

text_blocks.snippet: COPD (Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease) reduces gas exchange efficiency in the lungs primarily due to damage to the airways and air sacs (alveoli). This damage hinders the flow of air in and out of the lungs and reduces the surface area available for oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange.

list.title: Airway Narrowing:
list.snippet: COPD causes inflammation and thickening of the airway walls, leading to narrowing and obstruction of airflow.

list.title: Mucus Production:
list.snippet: Increased mucus production in the airways can also block airflow, further restricting gas exchange.

list.title: Airway Collapse:
list.snippet: In emphysema, a type of COPD, the walls of the alveoli are destroyed, and the airways can collapse during exhalation, trapping air and hindering the inflow of fresh air.

list.title: Reduced Surface Area:
list.snippet: The alveoli are where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged between the lungs and the blood. In COPD, the destruction of alveolar walls reduces the total surface area available for this exchange.

list.title: Impaired Gas Diffusion:
list.snippet: The damage to the alveoli and airways makes it harder for oxygen to pass into the blood and for carbon dioxide to be removed.

list.title: Uneven Airflow:
list.snippet: COPD can cause an uneven distribution of airflow to different parts of the lungs, meaning some areas receive more air than others.

list.title: Impaired Blood Flow:
list.snippet: Similarly, blood flow to different parts of the lungs may also be uneven. This mismatch between airflow and blood flow (ventilation-perfusion mismatch) further impairs gas exchange.
Hypoxemia: Reduced oxygen levels in the blood (hypoxemia).
Hypercapnia: Increased carbon dioxide levels in the blood (hypercapnia).
Shortness of Breath: The body compensates by increasing breathing rate and effort, leading to shortness of breath.
Fatigue: The body works harder to breathe, leading to fatigue.
